texts.0: SP, due to a rushed rotation input that was not referenced to the calculated takeoff data, did not execute the T/O with the standard airspeed. On one attempt the aircraft was held on the runway to more than 10 kt above the computed rotation speed and on another it was unstuck below that speed, where no tolerance exists. IP intervened on the stick and the power lever to re-establish the lift-off airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted scan of the airspeed indicator during the ground roll, held the aircraft on the runway until the airspeed had built to about 10 kt above the computed rotation speed, at the outer boundary of the takeoff band. The rotation was started only after IP called the speed, and the excess was carried into the initial climb. No control intervention was required, but the correction depended entirely on the verbal prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a late transition of the scan from the runway to the airspeed indicator, allowed the speed at rotation to reach roughly 8 kt above the computed value, outside the 5 kt band but inside the outer limit. SP recognized the excess without prompting and rotated smoothly, so the deviation was not carried into the initial climb.
texts.3: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed, rotating within 5 kt of the computed rotation speed taken from the calculated takeoff data. Lift-off was smooth and the airspeed trend was controlled through the transition to the climb.
texts.4: SP rotated at the computed takeoff speed with a deviation of no more than 1-2 kt, using a single continuous back-pressure input. The airspeed trend at lift-off was controlled so precisely that no further correction was needed in the transition to the climb.
texts.marginal: SP kept the takeoff airspeed within the standard, but the rotation consistently occurred at the upper edge of the band, close to 5 kt above the computed speed. The trend indicates that SP is waiting for the aircraft to feel ready instead of flying to the computed number. SP is expected to anchor the rotation on the calculated takeoff data and reduce the scatter on the following sorties.

texts_at.0: SP brought the aircraft to rotation with IP calling the computed rotation speed and confirming the back-pressure input alongside SP, due to this being one of the first takeoffs SP has flown to a computed rotation speed rather than by feel. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to confirm more of the rotation speed independently, with IP calling only as a backstop, on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP rotated about 9 kt above the computed rotation speed, at the edge of the standard, due to the airspeed scan being confirmed only as the aircraft was already lifting off. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the airspeed against the computed figure before, not as, the aircraft lifts off.
texts_at.2: SP rotated about 7 kt above the computed rotation speed, due to a scan that returned to the airspeed indicator a beat after the runway picture had already settled. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to return the scan to the airspeed indicator earlier in the ground roll.
texts_at.3: SP rotated about 4 kt above the computed rotation speed, due to the transition from the runway picture to the airspeed indicator being made a fraction later than it needed to be. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make the transition to the airspeed indicator a fraction earlier in the roll.

texts_above.1: SP rotated about 9 kt above the computed rotation speed, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP rotated within about 7 kt of the computed rotation speed, recognizing the excess without prompting and keeping the deviation clear of the initial climb. Moving the scan to the airspeed indicator a beat earlier in the roll would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good rotation-airspeed discipline.
texts_above.3: SP rotated within about 4 kt of the computed rotation speed, with the airspeed trend controlled smoothly through the transition to the climb. The only refinement available was to confirm the airspeed a moment earlier still in the roll. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good rotation-airspeed discipline.
texts_above.4: SP rotated at the computed takeoff speed with a deviation of no more than 1 to 2 kt, using a single continuous back-pressure input with the airspeed trend controlled precisely through the transition to the climb. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent rotation-airspeed discipline.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline maintenance during takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient and late rudder input against the swing that developed with power application, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Lateral displacement exceeded 10 ft and continued to diverge toward the runway edge as speed increased. IP took over the rudder to re-establish the takeoff path.
texts.1: SP, due to coarse and alternating rudder inputs, allowed lateral displacement from the centerline to reach about 10 ft, at the outer limit for the ground roll. The aircraft was brought back toward the centerline only after IP called for rudder, and the correction lagged the deviation. Directional control was recovered without any intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to delayed recognition of the initial drift after brake release, allowed the aircraft to displace some 7-8 ft from the centerline during the acceleration phase. SP identified the drift without prompting and applied progressive rudder that returned the aircraft to the centerline well before rotation.
texts.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline throughout the takeoff roll, keeping lateral displacement inside 5 ft with small and timely rudder corrections. Directional control remained positive from brake release to lift-off.
texts.4: SP tracked the centerline with a displacement that was barely perceptible, of the order of 1-2 ft, using anticipatory rather than corrective rudder. The same precision was retained through the power application and the rotation.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the runway centerline within the standard, but the aircraft settled on a constant 4-5 ft offset for most of the roll instead of tracking the line. The trend indicates that SP accepts a stabilized offset rather than correcting back to zero. SP is expected to fly the centerline as the reference and keep the residual displacement close to nil.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the runway centerline during the takeoff roll with IP calling the rudder corrections needed to hold the line, due to this being one of the first takeoff rolls SP has steered with rudder alone rather than with a demonstrated hand on the controls. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to hold more of the centerline independently, with IP calling only as a backstop, on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the aircraft about 9 ft from the centerline at the edge of the standard, due to a rudder correction that was sized once early in the roll and not refined as the drift continued. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refine the rudder correction as the roll continues rather than sizing it once.
texts_at.2: SP held the aircraft about 7 ft from the centerline, due to the initial drift after brake release being confirmed only after it had grown for a moment. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to confirm the initial drift the instant it starts rather than after it grows.
texts_at.3: SP held the aircraft about 4 ft from the centerline, due to a rudder correction that closed most, but not quite all, of the initial drift on the first application. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the first rudder correction to close the whole of the initial drift.

texts_above.1: SP held the aircraft about 9 ft from the centerline at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP held the aircraft within about 7 ft of the centerline, identifying the drift without prompting and applying progressive rudder that returned it to the centerline well before rotation. Sizing the first correction to close the whole of the drift, rather than most of it, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound centerline tracking.
texts_above.3: SP held the aircraft within about 4 ft of the centerline throughout the roll, with directional control positive from brake release to lift-off. The only refinement available was to anticipate the very first drift a fraction earlier still. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed centerline tracking.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the centerline with a displacement of only 1 to 2 ft, using anticipatory rather than corrective rudder, with the same precision retained through the power application and the rotation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional centerline tracking.

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in which briefed items were omitted under the workload of the runway entry, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions. More than one item of the check was left unaddressed and the aircraft was lined up for takeoff in that state. IP stopped the sequence and required the check to be repeated before power was applied.
texts.1: SP, due to an inadvertent slip in the flow of the LINE UP checks, passed over one item and did not detect the omission. The check was completed only after IP named the missing item on the runway. The takeoff itself was normal, but the trap came entirely from the verbal prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to interruption of the LINE UP flow by the tower transmission, initially skipped one item of the check. SP recognized the gap without prompting, went back over the flow and completed the check before brake release, with only a short delay to the takeoff.
texts.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and in the published sequence, completing them before the takeoff clearance was accepted. The flow was uninterrupted and the aircraft was correctly configured for T/O.
texts.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and at a pace that absorbed the tower transmission without breaking the flow. Each item was verified against the corresponding indication rather than recited, and the aircraft was ready for takeoff with nothing left outstanding.
texts.marginal: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions, but the flow was slow enough that the last items were completed after the aircraft was already aligned and holding on the runway. The trend indicates that the check is run reactively rather than in step with the runway entry. SP is expected to complete the flow without extending runway occupancy time.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the LINE UP checks with IP reading each item and confirming the aircraft is configured for takeoff alongside SP, due to this being one of the first times SP has run this check flow independently of a full walk-through. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to read and confirm more of the LINE UP items independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions, due to one item being confirmed only after the tower transmission had already been answered rather than in its published place. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm every item in its published place, not after an interruption is answered.
texts_at.2: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions, due to one item being verified a beat after the flow moved past it rather than in the same step. texts_at.3: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions, due to the flow pausing briefly on one item before the corresponding indication was confirmed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm each indication without the brief pause on the way through.

texts_above.1: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions and in the published sequence, absorbing the tower transmission without breaking the flow and completing before brake release. Removing the one brief pause on the way through the flow would make the sequence uniformly smooth. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid line-up check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omissions, with each item verified against the corresponding indication rather than recited and the aircraft ready for takeoff with nothing outstanding. The only refinement available was to close the runway occupancy time by a further second or two. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed line-up check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions at a pace that absorbed the tower transmission without breaking the flow, with every item verified against the corresponding indication and the aircraft ready for takeoff with nothing left outstanding. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding line-up check discipline.

error_modes.label: Aircraft held stationary during engine run-up

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient brake pressure held while power was advanced, allowed the A/C to creep forward during the engine run-up. The movement continued while the engine indications were being read and the run-up position was lost. IP applied the brakes and required the run-up to be repeated from a stopped position.
texts.1: SP, due to relaxation of the toe brakes when attention shifted to the engine instruments, allowed a clearly perceptible forward movement of the A/C during the run-up. Braking was reapplied only after IP called the movement, and the checks were finished from a displaced position on the runway.
texts.2: SP, due to an uneven brake application as the power lever was advanced, allowed a small forward movement at the start of the run-up. SP detected the movement immediately, restored full brake pressure and completed the engine checks with the aircraft stationary.
texts.3: SP did not allow any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, holding firm and symmetric brake pressure while power was advanced. The engine indications were checked with the aircraft completely stopped.
texts.4: SP held the A/C stationary throughout the run-up, with brake pressure set before power application and maintained without variation. The engine checks were completed within the normal time and the aircraft did not move at any point.
texts.marginal: SP prevented any movement of the A/C during the run-up, but only by increasing brake pressure after the power had already been advanced. The trend indicates that the braking is reacting to the thrust instead of preceding it. SP is expected to set the brakes fully before advancing power on the following sorties.

texts_at.0: SP ran the engine run-up with IP demonstrating the brake pressure needed before power was advanced and confirming the aircraft stayed stationary alongside SP, due to this being one of the first run-ups SP has held stationary without a demonstrated brake set beforehand. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to set more of the brake pressure independently before power is advanced on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the A/C stationary through the run-up, due to brake pressure being increased just after power began advancing rather than set fully before it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set full brake pressure before, not after, power begins advancing.
texts_at.2: SP held the A/C stationary through the run-up, due to brake pressure being confirmed only as power passed through the middle of the run-up range. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm brake pressure before power reaches the middle of the range.
texts_at.3: SP held the A/C stationary through the run-up, due to one brief check of brake pressure part-way through rather than a single confirmation held from the start. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the brake-pressure confirmation from the start rather than checking part-way.

texts_above.1: SP held the A/C stationary through the run-up. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP held the A/C stationary through the run-up, detecting a small forward tendency immediately, restoring full brake pressure and completing the engine checks with the aircraft stationary throughout. Setting the full brake pressure before power begins advancing, rather than just after, would remove the last reactive element. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady run-up brake discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the A/C stationary throughout the run-up with brake pressure set before power application and maintained without variation, the engine indications checked with the aircraft completely stopped. The only refinement available was to hold the confirmed brake pressure a beat longer into the highest part of the run-up. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate run-up brake discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the A/C stationary throughout the run-up with brake pressure set before power application and maintained without variation, the engine checks completed within the normal time with no movement at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary run-up brake discipline.

error_modes.label: Takeoff attitude at rotation and lift-off

texts.0: SP, due to an over-controlled pitch input at rotation, did not bring the A/C to the proper T/O attitude nor maintain it. The pitch oscillated after lift-off and the resulting airspeed departed the takeoff band by more than 10 kt. IP took the controls to stabilize the attitude and the initial climb.
texts.1: SP, due to an abrupt back-pressure input followed by an immediate relaxation, set a takeoff attitude that was not held, and the resulting airspeed excursion reached the 10 kt outer boundary. The attitude was stabilized only after IP called for a fixed pitch reference. No intervention on the controls was needed, but the correction was late.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch input made without a firm external reference, initially set a takeoff attitude slightly higher than required and the airspeed fell outside the 5 kt band. SP read the discrepancy from the airspeed trend and re-established the proper attitude without prompting, before the departure path was affected.
texts.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with a single smooth input and maintained it through the lift-off. Pitch was held against a defined reference and the airspeed stayed inside the 5 kt band.
texts.4: SP established the proper T/O attitude at the exact rotation point and held it with no perceptible pitch variation. The transition from ground roll to flight was continuous, with airspeed deviations of only 1-2 kt.
texts.marginal: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude and kept the parameters inside the standard, but the attitude needed two small corrections before it settled. The trend indicates that the initial pitch input is set approximately and then adjusted by feel. SP is expected to set the attitude once against the external reference and hold it.

texts_at.0: SP brought the aircraft toward the takeoff attitude with IP setting the initial pitch reference and confirming the resulting airspeed alongside SP, due to this being one of the first rotations SP has flown to an external attitude reference rather than by feel. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to set more of the pitch reference independently, with IP confirming the airspeed, on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with the resulting airspeed held to about 9 kt inside the standard, due to the first pitch input being set approximately before the external reference was used to refine it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the pitch input against the external reference the first time, not after it.
texts_at.2: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with the airspeed held to about 7 kt inside the standard, due to one small correction needed after the initial input before the attitude settled. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to settle the attitude on the initial input without the small correction that follows it.
texts_at.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with the airspeed held to about 4 kt inside the standard, due to the attitude being confirmed against the reference a fraction after it was set rather than as it was set. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm the attitude against the reference in the same motion it is set.

texts_above.1: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with the resulting airspeed held to about 9 kt inside the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with a single smooth input, the resulting airspeed held to about 7 kt inside the standard and no further correction needed through the lift-off. Confirming the attitude against the reference in the same motion it is set would remove the last small correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable rotation-attitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with a single smooth input and maintained it through the lift-off, airspeed held to about 4 kt inside the standard throughout. The only refinement available was to hold the confirmed attitude a shade more precisely through the lift-off itself. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good rotation-attitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP established the proper T/O attitude at the exact rotation point and held it with no perceptible pitch variation, the transition from ground roll to flight continuous with airspeed deviations of only 1 to 2 kt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior rotation-attitude discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a climb attitude chased on the airspeed indicator instead of being set against the horizon, did not bring the A/C to the proper climbing attitude nor maintain it. Pitch wandered continuously and the climb airspeed diverged beyond the 10 kt outer limit. IP intervened to establish and hold the correct climb attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to trimming the aircraft before the climb attitude had been stabilized, allowed the pitch to drift and the climb airspeed to reach the 10 kt outer boundary. The attitude was corrected only after IP gave repeated verbal references for pitch. The deviation persisted through the first part of the departure.
texts.2: SP, due to a climb attitude initially set low for the configuration, allowed the airspeed to move some 7 kt outside the computed climb value, past the 5 kt band. SP recognized the trend without prompting and re-set the pitch attitude, returning the airspeed inside the standard before the first turn.
texts.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude immediately after lift-off and maintained it, keeping the climb airspeed inside 5 kt of the standard value. Pitch and trim were stabilized without further corrections.
texts.4: SP set the proper climbing attitude in one movement and held it with variations of no more than 1-2 kt in airspeed. The aircraft was trimmed as soon as the attitude was established, and the climb required no further pitch input.
texts.marginal: SP established and maintained the proper climbing attitude inside the standard, but the pitch was allowed to settle over several seconds before it stabilized. The trend indicates that the target attitude is being approached gradually instead of being set directly. SP is expected to place the aircraft on the climb attitude at once and trim from there.

texts_at.0: SP established the climb attitude with IP setting the initial pitch and trim and confirming the resulting climb airspeed alongside SP, due to this being one of the first climb-outs SP has flown to a demonstrated attitude rather than an assigned one. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to set more of the climb attitude and trim independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude with the climb airspeed held to about 9 kt inside the standard, due to the pitch being allowed to settle gradually over several seconds rather than being set directly. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the climb attitude directly rather than letting it settle gradually.
texts_at.2: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude with the climb airspeed held to about 7 kt inside the standard, due to the pitch being trimmed a beat before it had fully stabilized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to let the pitch fully stabilize before it is trimmed.
texts_at.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude with the climb airspeed held to about 4 kt inside the standard, due to a short settling period before the attitude was confirmed against the reference. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to confirm the attitude against the reference without the short settling period.

texts_above.1: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude with the climb airspeed held to about 9 kt inside the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude immediately after lift-off, the climb airspeed held to about 7 kt inside the standard with pitch and trim stabilized without further correction. Setting the attitude directly, without the gradual settling period, would sharpen the transition further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured climb-attitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper climbing attitude immediately after lift-off and maintained it, the climb airspeed held to about 4 kt inside the standard with no further pitch input needed. The only refinement available was to trim the aircraft in the same instant the attitude was set. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise climb-attitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP set the proper climbing attitude in one movement and held it with variations of no more than 1 to 2 kt in airspeed, trimmed as soon as the attitude was established with no further pitch input required. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate climb-attitude discipline.

error_modes.label: Configuration cleanup within speed limits (L/G and flaps)

texts.0: SP, due to an absent cross-check of the aircraft state against the primary flight instruments after lift-off, selected L/G and flaps up without reference to the airspeed and did not clean the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit. The published limiting speed was exceeded while the aircraft was still accelerating. IP intervened on the power lever and the pitch attitude to bring the airspeed back inside the limit.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed outside the cockpit, delayed the retraction of L/G and flaps until the airspeed was at the published limit for the configuration. The selections were made only after IP called the speed, and no margin remained. Cleaning of the configuration was completed without any intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that returned late to the airspeed indicator after lift-off, allowed the acceleration to run further than planned before the retraction was selected. SP detected the trend without prompting and completed the cleanup with a small margin to the limiting speed, holding pitch to arrest the acceleration.
texts.3: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating any speed limit, selecting L/G and flaps up at the correct points with a clear margin to the limiting speeds. The airspeed was cross-checked before each selection and the indications were confirmed.
texts.4: SP retracted L/G and flaps at precisely the correct points with a comfortable margin to the limiting speeds, each selection preceded by a positive airspeed cross-check and followed by confirmation of the indications. The cleanup did not disturb the climb attitude or the airspeed trend.
texts.marginal: SP cleaned the A/C configuration inside the speed limits, but each selection was made with only a small margin remaining to the limiting speed. The trend indicates that the retractions are being timed on aircraft feel rather than on the indicated airspeed. SP is expected to cross-check the speed earlier and restore a comfortable margin on the following sorties.

texts_at.0: SP retracted the landing gear and the flaps with IP calling the airspeed cross-check before each selection and confirming the margin to the limiting speed, due to this being one of the first configuration cleanups SP has sequenced against the airspeed indicator rather than against a called cue. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to cross-check more of the selections independently, with IP confirming the margin, on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit, due to one retraction being selected with only a narrow margin remaining before the airspeed cross-check confirmed it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the airspeed cross-check before, not as, the margin narrows.
texts_at.2: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit, due to the acceleration being allowed to run a little further than planned before one retraction was selected. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to select each retraction at the planned point rather than letting the acceleration run on.
texts_at.3: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit, due to one selection following its airspeed cross-check by a fraction rather than in the same instant. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to select the retraction in the same instant as its airspeed cross-check.

texts_above.1: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating any speed limit, selecting L/G and flaps up with a clear margin to the limiting speeds and the airspeed cross-checked before each selection. Selecting the one retraction in the same instant as its cross-check, rather than a fraction after, would widen the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent configuration-cleanup discipline.
texts_above.3: SP selected L/G and flaps up at the correct points with a clear margin to the limiting speeds on every selection, each preceded by a positive airspeed cross-check with the indications confirmed. The only refinement available was to hold a slightly wider margin on the single fastest selection. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined configuration-cleanup discipline.
texts_above.4: SP retracted L/G and flaps at precisely the correct points with a comfortable margin to the limiting speeds, each selection preceded by a positive airspeed cross-check and followed by confirmation of the indications, with the cleanup disturbing neither the climb attitude nor the airspeed trend. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless configuration-cleanup discipline.

error_modes.label: Acceleration to and maintenance of standard climb airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude that was not adjusted as the configuration changed, did not accelerate the A/C to the standard climb airspeed nor maintain it. The airspeed diverged by more than 10 kt from the standard value and continued to drift as the departure progressed. IP took the controls to set the attitude and stabilize the climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an untrimmed aircraft after the cleanup, allowed the climb airspeed to move out to the 10 kt outer boundary of the standard value. The airspeed was recovered only after repeated verbal references from the IP, and the aircraft was still not trimmed at the end of the departure segment. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed trim input following flap retraction, allowed the climb airspeed to deviate by some 7 kt from the standard value, outside the 5 kt band. SP recognized the deviation without prompting, corrected the pitch attitude and re-trimmed, restoring the standard climb airspeed promptly.
texts.3: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed and maintained it inside 5 kt, trimming the aircraft as soon as the configuration was clean. The acceleration from brake release to the climb speed was continuous and controlled.
texts.4: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed and held it with deviations of no more than 1-2 kt, with the aircraft trimmed hands-off. The acceleration profile matched the calculated takeoff data throughout.
texts.marginal: SP accelerated to and maintained the standard climb airspeed within the standard, but the speed was held consistently at the upper edge of the allowed band. The trend indicates that the pitch attitude is being set slightly low and then accepted. SP is expected to fly the standard climb airspeed as the target rather than as a boundary.

texts_at.0: SP accelerated the aircraft toward the standard climb airspeed with IP setting the initial pitch and trimming the aircraft alongside SP, due to this being one of the first climb accelerations SP has trimmed for hands-off rather than held with continuous pressure. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to trim more of the climb independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed and held it to about 9 kt inside the standard, due to a trim input following flap retraction by a beat rather than in the same motion. error_modes.label: Crosswind controls not released after lift-off (upwind wing dips instead of crabbing)

texts.0: SP, due to the crosswind controls being held after takeoff instead of released, did not allow the A/C to crab into the wind and the upwind wing dipped towards the ground just after lift-off. The A/C left the extended runway centerline downwind and the climb was flown uncoordinated with the wing low. IP took the controls to level the wings and re-establish the takeoff leg.
texts.1: SP, due to into-wind aileron and rudder carried into the initial climb, did not transition to a crab and the upwind wing stayed low. The A/C drifted to the outer limit of the lateral tolerance off the extended centerline before the controls were neutralized, which happened only after IP called for the crosswind controls to be released. No control intervention was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed release of the crosswind controls after the wheels left the ground, held the upwind wing low for a few seconds of the initial climb. The A/C drifted some 7 feet off the extended centerline, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP released the inputs without prompting, established the crab and regained runway alignment early on the takeoff leg.
texts.3: SP released the crosswind controls at lift-off and allowed the A/C to crab into the wind, keeping the wings level and the flight coordinated. Runway alignment on the takeoff leg was maintained inside 5 feet of the extended centerline.
texts.4: SP blended the release of the crosswind controls into the rotation itself, so the A/C passed from the wing-low ground correction to a coordinated crab in one continuous movement. No wing dip occurred, the ball stayed centered and the extended centerline was tracked exactly.
texts.marginal: SP flew the crosswind departure inside standards, but the ground crosswind inputs were relaxed gradually over the first seconds of climb rather than released at lift-off, leaving the upwind wing slightly low. The trend indicates the ground-to-air transition of the wind correction is not yet a distinct action. SP is expected to release the crosswind controls at lift-off and crab into the wind.

texts_at.0: SP released the crosswind controls after lift-off with IP calling the timing of the release and confirming the transition to a crab, due to this being one of the first crosswind departures SP has flown transitioning from a wing-low ground correction to a crab. texts_at.2: SP kept the A/C within about 7 ft of the extended centerline on the takeoff leg, due to a delayed release of the crosswind controls that held the upwind wing low for a few seconds of the climb. error_modes.label: Right rudder trim not applied after safe gear retraction (ball off center)

texts.0: SP, due to right rudder trim not being applied immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction, left the adverse yaw untrimmed and the ball out of center for the whole initial climb. The uncoordinated climb produced a continuous drift off the departure track and a foot load that also disturbed the pitch and airspeed control beyond the takeoff band. IP took the controls to trim the A/C and re-establish the climb.
texts.1: SP, due to the after-takeoff rudder trim being omitted, held the A/C uncoordinated with pedal pressure and let the heading wander to the outer limit of the tolerance on the takeoff leg. The trim was set only after IP called for right rudder trim and centered ball, and the climb parameters were regained late. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to right rudder trim applied several seconds after gear retraction, flew part of the initial climb with the ball off center and a drift building off the extended centerline. The deviation reached an intermediate value between the code 3 and code 1 limits before SP noticed the pedal pressure without prompting, trimmed the adverse yaw out and recentered the ball.
texts.3: SP applied some right rudder trim immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction, counteracting adverse yaw and centering the ball. The climb was flown coordinated and free of pedal pressure, with the departure track and airspeed held inside the standard.
texts.4: SP set the right rudder trim as part of the after-takeoff flow, with the ball centered before the first climb crosscheck and no residual pedal pressure at any time. The A/C tracked the extended centerline exactly and the climb parameters showed only negligible variation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the initial climb inside standards, but the right rudder trim was applied only after the pedal pressure became noticeable, so the ball was slightly off center for the first part of the climb. The trend indicates the trim is being set by feel rather than as a fixed after-takeoff action. SP is expected to trim out the adverse yaw immediately after safe gear retraction.

texts_at.0: SP applied right rudder trim after gear retraction with IP calling the timing of the trim input relative to the pedal pressure, due to this being one of the first initial climbs SP has flown trimming out adverse yaw as a fixed after-takeoff action rather than by feel. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to apply more of the rudder trim independently as a fixed action on the next sortie.

texts_at.2: SP held the extended centerline within about 7 ft on the initial climb, due to right rudder trim being applied several seconds after gear retraction rather than as part of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply right rudder trim as part of gear retraction, not several seconds after.
texts_at.3: SP held the extended centerline within about 4 ft on the initial climb, due to the trim being set a fraction after the pedal pressure was first noticed rather than in the same motion. error_modes.label: Takeoff point not planned for wake turbulence of the preceding A/C

texts.0: SP, due to wake turbulence not being anticipated when taking off behind another A/C on the same runway with the wind straight down the runway, did not plan a lift-off point prior to the preceding A/C's takeoff point. The A/C rotated into the wake and the resulting roll and yaw took it well off the departure track with the wings not level below 500 feet. IP took the controls to fly clear of the wake.
texts.1: SP, due to no assessment of the preceding A/C's takeoff point, accepted a lineup and roll that placed the lift-off inside the wake area. The A/C was displaced to the outer limit of the lateral tolerance on the takeoff leg and the wings were leveled only after IP called the wake encounter and the correction. No intervention on the controls was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to the wake turbulence plan being made only after lineup rather than while anticipating the departure, started the roll from a position that gave little margin on the preceding A/C's takeoff point. SP recognized this without prompting and rotated early enough to stay above the wake, accepting an intermediate airspeed deviation of some 7 kt above the computed rotation speed.
texts.3: SP anticipated wake turbulence from the preceding A/C on the same runway and planned to become airborne prior to its takeoff point. The takeoff was flown clear of the wake with rotation inside 5 kt of the computed speed and the departure track maintained.
texts.4: SP identified the preceding A/C's takeoff point during the pattern scan, briefed the intended lift-off point before lineup and flew the takeoff exactly to that plan. The A/C stayed clear of the wake throughout, with rotation speed and departure track showing only negligible deviation.
texts.marginal: SP flew the takeoff inside standards and clear of the wake, but the takeoff point of the preceding A/C was noted only when the lineup clearance was received. The trend indicates that wake turbulence is being handled reactively rather than planned from the position reports in the pattern. SP is expected to plan the lift-off point relative to the preceding A/C before taxiing onto the runway.

texts_at.0: SP flew the takeoff behind another aircraft with IP calling the preceding aircraft's takeoff point and the intended lift-off point relative to the wake, due to this being one of the first takeoffs SP has planned specifically to stay clear of a preceding aircraft's wake. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to plan more of the wake-clearance lift-off point independently on the next sortie.

The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to note the preceding A/C's takeoff point earlier in the pattern, not only at the lineup clearance.
texts_at.2: SP rotated about 7 kt above the computed rotation speed to stay clear of the wake, due to the wake turbulence plan being made only after lineup rather than while anticipating the departure. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to confirm the margin on the preceding A/C's point as early as it is available.
